title: An easy way to give kids more freedom
gist: Yglesias uses his son's new bus commute to middle school to argue Apple should let kids' Apple Watch accounts load digital transit passes, and more broadly that Big Tech underinvests in products that solve real parent/family problems despite the reputational upside of doing so.

insights.claim: Apple's Watch 'kids' mode' (which pairs a child's watch to a parent's iPhone without a full smartphone) currently blocks loading a digital mass-transit pass into the child's Apple Wallet, even though the feature exists for adult accounts.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A narrow, low-cost product/policy fix (removing an age gate) could materially improve Apple Watch's value proposition for the large parent/family segment choosing watches over smartphones for tweens.
insights.quote: kids’ mode prevents you from loading a transit pass into a kid’s version of the Apple Wallet. That seems crazy!
insights.locator: Many sixth graders have smartphones these days

insights.claim: Apple has no dedicated hardware products designed from the ground up for children, instead relying on software-level restrictions like Apple Watch kids' mode, which the author attributes to Apple calculating that a kid-specific device would have low incremental ROI given how many kids already use existing Apple products.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Signals an underserved product niche (family/child-oriented hardware) that a Big Tech company willing to invest could capture, especially if it also buys back consumer trust.
insights.locator: You see this most obviously in the fact that the Apple hardware ecosystem doesn't have any dedicated products for kids

themes.theme: The 'bloody R.O.I.' framework for durable company culture

insights.claim: In 2014, then-Apple-CEO Tim Cook told a shareholder challenging the ROI of accessibility features for blind users, 'When we work on making our devices accessible by the blind, I don't consider the bloody R.O.I.,' adding that ROI-only investors 'should get out of this stock.'
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Illustrates a real-world case where a public company's CEO explicitly deprioritized ROI on a customer-facing investment and was rewarded with a durable brand/talent advantage — a template for evaluating whether other 'mission over margin' corporate stances are actually shareholder-friendly long-run.
insights.quote: When we work on making our devices accessible by the blind, I don’t consider the bloody R.O.I. If you want me to do things only for R.O.I. reasons, you should get out of this stock.

insights.claim: A company's willingness to fund low-direct-ROI initiatives that visibly make the world better is a cheap way to attract and retain talent, because employees are more willing to do difficult, diligent work when they believe it serves a purpose beyond profit.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Useful lens for assessing tech-company hiring/retention risk: firms perceived as purely extractive (e.g., over addictive engagement optimization) may face a rising talent-cost penalty relative to those seen as mission-aligned.
insights.locator: It’s a lot cheaper and easier to attract and retain people

insights.claim: The tech industry underrates how much genuine enthusiasm existed about its work 10-15 years ago, and how much of that goodwill has eroded — not from external propaganda, but from the industry's own realization that addictive video-recommendation algorithms don't align with society's (or parents') aspirations.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Frames a reputational/regulatory tail risk for platform companies built on engagement-maximizing recommendation algorithms (e.g., Meta, YouTube/Alphabet, TikTok/ByteDance), and a potential brand-rehabilitation opportunity for whichever company pivots hardest toward solving real family problems.
insights.locator: I kind of think that this is a mistake

themes.theme: Mass transit as a child-independence unlock

insights.claim: Mass transit dramatically extends the effective independent range of children in cities in a way that large suburban yards and playrooms cannot replace, letting kids outgrow toy-based play and begin navigating urban space with peers.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Supports a pro-transit, pro-density argument relevant to urban real estate and municipal transit-funding debates: family retention in cities is tied to transit quality, not just school quality.
insights.locator: mass transit is an incredible unlock for older kids

insights.claim: A fare-evasion crackdown on WMATA's Metro rail system led to a noticeable improvement in rider conditions, and WMATA extended the same enforcement approach to its bus system starting in spring 2026.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A concrete, replicable transit-agency policy lever (fare enforcement) that other US transit systems could use to boost perceived safety and mainstream ridership, which in turn supports property values and ridership-dependent transit revenue near well-run systems.
insights.quote: The situation on the Metro dramatically improved after a fare evasion crackdown, and since this past spring, WMATA has brought that same energy to the bus.
insights.locator: I don’t want to overly idealize WMATA

insights.claim: Transit systems are only a positive unlock for kids' independence when they have high ridership and mainstream commuter usage; low-ridership routes in transit-poor areas would not serve the same purpose and shouldn't be used as justification for building transit where no one rides it.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A caveat for transit-expansion investment theses: ridership levels, not route existence alone, determine whether new transit lines generate the family/child-safety network effects that support long-run ridership growth.
insights.locator: this is not really a reason to build mass-transit infrastructure

insights.claim: The author's 11-year-old son now independently rides a low-frequency city bus a few blocks from home to a middle school across town, alongside other neighborhood peers who form a reliable cohort on the one bus timed to arrive before school starts.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Concrete illustration of how transit-dependent family logistics function even with imperfect (low-frequency) service, relevant to how transit agencies and developers might market family-friendly transit-oriented development.
insights.locator: we decided to take a great leap forward in child autonomy
